name: George E. Shibley
bio: George E. Shibley was a California labor and civil-liberties attorney who, after a jury acquitted him of contempt of a military court and of a related felony, was convicted of 'summary contempt' and sentenced to three years and disbarment for his vigorous defense of an enlisted Marine. Supporters said the prosecution, ordered from Washington, was meant solely to punish a civilian lawyer; his case was on appeal to the Supreme Court.
charges: Summary contempt of court — arising from his defense of an enlisted serviceman
convicted: Convicted; on appeal to the Supreme Court

name: Harold I. Cammer
bio: Harold I. Cammer was a New York labor attorney held in contempt of court for his conduct in defending the fur-union leader Ben Gold against a Taft-Hartley charge. The U.S. Supreme Court reversed his contempt conviction in March 1956.
charges: Contempt of court — arising from defending a Taft-Hartley defendant
convicted: Convicted; reversed by the Supreme Court March 1956

name: John H. Calhoun
bio: John H. Calhoun was the head of Atlanta's NAACP, jailed for contempt in 1956 for refusing to hand over the organization's books to Georgia state revenue agents in the state's drive to tax the NAACP out of existence. He was released after four hours and given a one-year suspended contempt sentence by a judge who openly avowed segregationist views.
charges: Contempt — for refusing to produce NAACP records to state agents
convicted: Jailed for contempt; one-year suspended sentence

name: J. Minor Sullivan
bio: Dr. J. Minor Sullivan III was a Black Trenton physician convicted of seven counts of perjury in February 1956 for testifying that the Trenton Six defendants had appeared drugged when they 'confessed' — testimony that helped expose the frame-up. His prosecution capped a years-long vendetta by prosecutor Mario Volpe, and he faced up to seven years.
charges: Perjury — for his exculpatory testimony in the Trenton Six case

name: A. A. Fisher
bio: A. A. Fisher was a Pacific Northwest leader of the International Woodworkers of America convicted of falsely signing a Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavit. The Ninth Circuit reversed his conviction in February 1956 — finding the trial judge had wrongly barred FBI records of payments to an informer and misdefined 'affiliation' — and the government announced it would retry him.
charges: Falsely signing a Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavit
convicted: Convicted; reversed on appeal February 1956; faced retrial

name: John J. Killian
bio: John J. Killian was a former United Electrical Workers official in Chicago convicted of filing a false Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavit.
charges: Falsely signing a Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavit
sentence: Convicted under the Taft-Hartley affidavit provision

name: John W. Powell
bio: John W. Powell was the editor and publisher of the China Monthly Review, a Shanghai magazine his family had run for decades, indicted in San Francisco in April 1956 on thirteen counts of sedition under a 1917 wartime statute. The charges rested on the Review's reporting that the Korean War was a tragic error and its accounts of U.S. bacteriological warfare; he called it a freedom-of-the-press case.
charges: Sedition (Espionage Act of 1917) — over his magazine's Korean War reporting
sentence: Faced up to 260 years across 13 counts; free on bail

name: Sylvia Powell
bio: Sylvia Powell was a co-defendant with her husband John W. Powell and Julian Schuman in the 1956 sedition prosecution over the China Monthly Review's reporting on the Korean War — one of the very few sedition cases the U.S. government brought against journalists in the period.
charges: Sedition (Espionage Act of 1917) — over the China Monthly Review's reporting

name: Julian Schuman
bio: Julian Schuman was a U.S. correspondent and staff writer for the China Monthly Review — the last American reporter to leave China — indicted with the Powells in 1956 for sedition over the magazine's coverage of the Korean War. He was the author of 'Assignment China.'
charges: Sedition (Espionage Act of 1917) — over the China Monthly Review's reporting

name: Anthony Minerich
bio: Anthony Minerich was a veteran coal-miners' organizer and business manager of the Croatian-language weekly Narodni Glasnik, stripped of his U.S. citizenship in a 1956 Chicago denaturalization trial. The government cited his Communist membership and a 1928 contempt conviction for addressing miners in defiance of a strike injunction; he had come to the U.S. at age two.
charges: Denaturalization — for past Communist membership and union activity
sentence: Loss of citizenship; faced deportation to Yugoslavia

name: Leo Fisher
bio: Leo Fisher was the editor of the Croatian-language weekly Narodni Glasnik in Chicago, denaturalized in 1956 in the same government drive against the paper's staff — his citizenship revoked over an arrest for leading a Depression-era unemployed demonstration.
charges: Denaturalization — over a Depression-era political arrest

name: Arthur Bartl
bio: Arthur Bartl was the assistant editor of the Croatian-language weekly Narodni Glasnik, facing denaturalization proceedings in 1956 as part of the government's drive against the paper's staff — though he had earned his citizenship through a wartime OSS mission behind Nazi lines.

name: Paul Brown
bio: Paul Brown (born Samuel Horowitz) was a Communist Party official who changed his name to avoid blacklisting and was then prosecuted for putting the new name on an automobile registration. He served six months in Minneapolis and spent nine more months fighting extradition to Milwaukee before a court dismissed the case in July 1956, ruling he had a lawful right to change his name with no intent to defraud.
charges: Auto-registration under a changed name — a pretext to prosecute a Communist
sentence: Six months served, plus a long extradition fight; case dismissed

name: Iva Toguri D'Aquino
bio: Iva Toguri D'Aquino — the Japanese-American woman the press dubbed 'Tokyo Rose' — was convicted of treason in 1949 over wartime radio broadcasts, on evidence a juror later called inconclusive. Paroled in January 1956 after serving her term, she was at once served with a deportation warrant in what would have been the first deportation of a natural-born U.S. citizen; eight civil-liberties lawyers took up her cause.
charges: Treason (1949); then an attempt to deport a natural-born U.S. citizen
sentence: Ten years served; then a deportation fight
